concepts.title: Many Ways to Move
concepts.explanation:
Before we talk about pushing and pulling other things, feel how your own body moves.

Stand up in a clear space. How many ways can you move?

Walk slowly, like a camel walking in the heat. Now walk fast. Which one was fast?

Jump up high. Did you notice what you did? You pushed the floor with your feet, and that push sent you up.

Turn around slowly, like a spinning top. Now you are turning.

Swing your arms back and forth, like a swing at the park.

Every one of those movements happened because something pushed or pulled. When you jump, your feet push the ground. When you swing your arms, your muscles pull them back and forth. Movement always starts with a push or a pull.
concepts.example: Stand up and move in four ways: walk, jump, turn and swing your arms. After each one, say whether you pushed or pulled to make it happen.

concepts.title: Push Moves Away, Pull Brings Near
concepts.explanation:
Here are the two big words of this unit: push and pull.

A push moves something away from you. A pull brings something closer to you. That is the whole idea, and it is easy to feel with your own hands.

Put a toy car on the floor. Push it away with one finger and say the word out loud: push! It went away from you.

Now tie a string to a small box and pull it towards you. Say: pull! It came to you.

Doors are a good place to spot both. You push a door to shut it. You pull a door to open it.

Say the word at the same time as you do the action. Push and say push. Pull and say pull. Doing it and saying it together helps you remember which is which.
concepts.example: Find a door. Push it shut and say push. Pull it open and say pull. Then find two more things at home that you push, and two that you pull.

concepts.title: Move, Stop, and Turn
concepts.explanation:
A push or a pull can do three different jobs. Many people think a push only makes things go — but it can do more than that.

The first job is to start something moving. Roll a ball across the floor. Your push made it move.

The second job is to stop something. When the ball rolls back to you, put your hand out. The ball stops. Your hand pushed it to stop.

The third job is to make something turn a new way. Roll the ball again, then push it gently from the side. It does not stop — it turns and travels in a new direction.

Try all three with a toy car. Push it to start. Block it to stop. Tap its side to make it turn.

A push or a pull can make a thing go, make a thing stop, and make a thing turn. With your pushes and pulls, you are the boss of the ball.
concepts.example: Roll a ball three times. First make it move, then stop it with your hand, then tap it from the side to make it turn.

concepts.title: Fast and Slow, Roll and Slide
concepts.explanation:
Now for two new ideas you can feel with your own hands.

The first idea is about how hard you push. A big push makes a thing go fast. A small push makes it go slow.

Give a ball a soft push and watch it travel slowly. Soft push, slow ball. Now give it a big push and watch it race away. Big push, fast ball. The size of your push decides the speed.

The second idea is about shape. Round things roll, and flat things slide.

Roll a ball or an orange along the floor. It rolls because it is round and has no corners to stop it.

Now push a shoe or a block. It does not roll — it slides along on its flat bottom.

So the shape of a thing changes how it moves when you push it.
concepts.example: Push a ball softly, then hard, and say which push made it faster. Then find one thing that rolls and one thing that slides.

concepts.title: Pushes and Pulls Around Us
concepts.explanation:
Pushes and pulls are everywhere. Once you know the two words, you start seeing them all day long.

Walk around your home and yard. At each thing you meet, ask yourself one question: do we push it, or pull it?

You push a chair in under the table. You pull a drawer out. You push a door shut and pull it open. You turn a tap.

Out in the yard there are more. You push a swing to send it away. You pull a toy cart behind you. You roll a ball with a push.

Watch a grown-up sweeping with a broom. Look carefully — that is a push and a pull, over and over again.

Out on the road, a camel or a donkey pulls a cart. The animal pulls, and the cart follows.

Science is not only in books. It is in your home, your yard and your road, all day long.
concepts.example: Walk around your home and find five things you push or pull. Say push or pull for each one as you find it.

commonMistakes: Only people can push and pull things.
Wind and water push things too — a breeze can push a boat along.
How fast something moves depends on how hard it is pushed or pulled.

connections.text: Pushing and pulling shows which materials bend, stretch or stay stiff.
Swings, slides and balls all move because of pushes and pulls.
